background.title: Literary and non-literary texts
background.html:
Literary texts are novels, poems and plays, like Purple Hibiscus. Non-literary texts are everyday texts made to inform, persuade or entertain: adverts, speeches, blogs, photographs, cartoons.

Paper 1 uses only non-literary texts you have never seen, so you cannot learn answers by heart. You learn a method for any text. Today you practise it on cartoons.

background.title: What it shows and what it means
background.html:
Every cartoon has two layers. Literal: what is there ("a man waters a small plant in front of smoking chimneys"). Implied: what you are meant to understand ("companies make small green gestures to hide big pollution").

A friend texting "Great, another Monday" literally praises Monday but implies the opposite. Marks come from explaining the implied layer and the details that lead you there.

background.title: Irony: when words and reality do not match
background.html: Irony is a gap between what is said or expected and what is true. Saying "lovely weather" in a storm is verbal irony. Cartoonists use it all the time: the speech bubble says one thing, the picture shows the opposite. Spot the gap and say what it reveals about the speaker. If you miss irony, you may think a cartoon agrees with the very thing it attacks.

background.title: Analysing is not retelling
background.html:
Retelling: "Two women sit in a café and one shows a photo." Anyone can see that.

Analysing: "The phone sits exactly between the friends, so the device comes between them, suggesting technology divides people."

Test: after each piece of evidence, does your sentence go on with so, because or which suggests? If it stops at the evidence, it is still retelling.

terms.def: Not seen before. In Paper 1 the texts are new to you in the exam, so you cannot prepare answers in advance, only the method.
Not a novel, poem or play. Non-literary texts are everyday texts such as adverts, speeches, blogs, photographs and cartoons.
The kind of text, such as an advert, a speech, a blog or a cartoon. Each type has its own usual features.
The question printed with each Paper 1 text. It points you to one aspect of how the text works, and your answer should keep coming back to it.
The standards your answer is marked against. Paper 1 has four, A to D, each worth 5 marks per text.
Higher Level and Standard Level. You take English at HL: more texts to study, both Paper 1 texts, and an extra HL essay.
How much a part of the assessment counts towards your final grade. Paper 1 is 35%: just over a third of your English grade.
Write short notes on or next to a text while you study it: circle details, label techniques, jot down ideas.
Using humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise someone or something, usually people with power. You laugh, then you judge.
A cartoon in the opinion pages of a newspaper or news site, about a real news issue, giving the cartoonist's point of view.
Gentle, amused satire that teases and invites people to laugh at a fault and change it. Named after the Roman poet Horace.
Harsh, angry satire that attacks something seen as seriously wrong. Named after the Roman poet Juvenal.
In satire, the person, group or idea being criticised.
What a reader needs to know around a text to understand it: the news story, the people, and when and where it was published.
A fixed phrase whose meaning is not the meaning of its words, such as "we're all in the same boat" (we share the same problem).
The writer's or cartoonist's attitude towards the subject or audience: mocking, serious, bitter, playful.
The atmosphere a text creates, the feeling it gives the audience: uneasy, cheerful, gloomy.
How formal the language is, from chatty to academic, and whose kind of voice it sounds like. Exam answers need a formal register.
The big idea underneath a text, such as inequality or loneliness, as opposed to what literally happens.
A drawing of a real person with some features stretched or shrunk to make a point, such as huge ears for someone who listens to nobody.
Showing something as bigger, smaller or more extreme than it is in real life, to make a point.
Using an object, animal or figure to stand for an idea. A dove stands for peace; a fat cat for a greedy rich person.
An idea drawn as if it were a real object, such as debt drawn as a ball and chain.
Showing an issue as a different situation that people already understand, so they judge it the same way: a government drawn as a crew arguing on a sinking ship.
Placing two contrasting things side by side so the reader compares them, such as rich next to poor.
A fixed, oversimplified idea about a whole group of people, such as "all teenagers are lazy".
Copying a famous image or text and changing it, to make fun of something or give the original a new meaning.
The line of text above or below a picture, or its title.
A joke using a word with two meanings at once, such as "going green" (turning green, and becoming eco-friendly).
A gap between what is said or expected and what is true. Verbal irony: saying "lovely weather" in a storm.
Deliberate overstatement in words: "I've told you a million times".
Making something sound much smaller than it is, such as calling a flood "a bit of rain".
A soft, polite word used to hide something unpleasant, such as "let go" for "sacked".
Technical words used by a particular group, which outsiders may not understand and which can hide what is really meant.
A short reference to a famous text, saying, story or person that the reader is expected to recognise.
One strong colour used against a plain or grey background, so the eye goes straight to it.
How strong or dull a colour is. Bright red is highly saturated; greyish red is not.
The plain surface meaning: what is actually shown or said, before any reading between the lines.
Suggested without being said directly. You work out an implied message from clues.
Your explanation of what a text means, supported by details from it. Different readers can give different, equally good interpretations.
Judging how well something works, with reasons: is the cartoon effective, and why?
The main argument of your whole answer, stated in the introduction, usually in one or two sentences.
The first sentence of a paragraph. It states the point the paragraph will prove.
Reading the picture and the words together, showing how they work as one, instead of in two separate lists.
A clever, less obvious point that shows deep understanding.
A sentence where the thing done to comes first and the doer is hidden or after "by": "His face is generated by AI" instead of "AI generates his face".
The last line of a joke, which makes it funny or gives it the twist.
The edges of the cartoon picture, and everything inside them.
An idea you cannot see or touch, such as freedom, debt or fear.
A paragraph pattern: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. The Horsey file names it but does not spell it out; this is the usual meaning.
Serious, careful language for school and work: no slang, no contractions like "don't", full sentences.
Your own collection of notes, analyses and reflections from the course. It is not graded, but the school keeps it and you use it to prepare for assessments.
The written-out words of something spoken, such as a video or a radio report.
A hormone (a chemical message in the body) that rises when you are stressed. Scientists measure it in saliva to see how stressed someone is.
When a doctor officially tells a patient to take a treatment, usually a medicine; here, a museum visit.
Guide the reader to see something from one side, so they share a certain view.
